extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and professionals interested in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing psychoanalytic theory and psychodynamic/psychoanalytic therapies, including empirical effectiveness, scientific status, methodological criticisms, and socio-cultural critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic effectiveness by disorder (INSERM 2004)
rubrics_metrics.description: INSERM (2004) concluded psychoanalysis was 'presumed or proven effective' at treating panic disorder, post-traumatic stress and personality disorders, but had 'little or no effect' on treating schizophrenia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate effectiveness separately by disorder using systematic reviews/meta-analyses; note that efficacy can vary widely across diagnostic categories and that blanket claims of effectiveness are not supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation via randomized controlled comparisons (APA 2011)
rubrics_metrics.description: The American Psychological Association (2011) made 103 comparisons between psychodynamic treatment and a non-dynamic competitor and found 6 were superior, 5 were inferior, 28 had no difference and 63 were adequate, suggesting a possible basis to consider psychodynamic psychotherapy 'empirically validated'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the body of RCT and comparison studies (number, direction of effects, and quality) when judging whether a psychodynamic approach meets empirical-validation standards; consider both superiority and non-inferiority outcomes and study quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect sizes from meta-analyses (STPP, I-STPP, LTPP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meta-analyses report effect sizes for Short Term Psychodynamic Psychotherapy (STPP) ranging from 34–71% compared to no treatment; somatic disorders 78–91%; depression 69%. Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (I-STPP) showed effect sizes from 84% (interpersonal problems) to 151% (depression), overall 118% vs no treatment. Long Term Psychodynamic Psychotherapy (LTPP) systematic review (2009) found overall effect size of 33% (other reviews 44–68%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reported effect sizes to judge magnitude of benefit compared to no-treatment or alternative treatments; interpret clinical significance, follow-up outcomes, and methodological heterogeneity in meta-analyses rather than relying on single summary numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative effectiveness versus other psychotherapies (e.g., CBT)
rubrics_metrics.description: A French 2004 report from INSERM stated psychoanalytic therapy is far less effective than other psychotherapies (including cognitive behavioral therapy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform head-to-head comparisons and network meta-analyses to compare psychoanalytic approaches to other established therapies (CBT, behavioural therapies); consider both short-term and long-term outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of outcomes on therapist quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous studies have shown that efficacy is related to the quality of the therapist, rather than the psychoanalytic school, technique, or training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating treatment effectiveness, account for therapist-level variables (competence, alliance-building, experience) and consider whether observed effects are attributable to modality-specific factors or therapist effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with scientific approaches and falsifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Karl Popper argued psychoanalysis is a pseudoscience because its claims are not testable and cannot be refuted (i.e., not falsifiable). Others (e.g., Grünbaum) argue psychoanalytic theories are falsifiable but that causal claims lack clinical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether theoretical claims are formulated so they can be empirically tested and potentially falsified; distinguish between interpretive/hypothesis-generating claims and those making causal therapeutic claims that require experimental confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of qualitative (case-study) versus quantitative/experimental research
rubrics_metrics.description: Early critics believed psychoanalytic theories relied too little on quantitative and experimental research and too much on qualitative clinical case studies; accusations include selective reporting or fabrication in historical cases (e.g., Anna O.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the methodological portfolio: the presence, quality, and replicability of controlled experimental studies and large-sample quantitative research versus reliance on single-case or clinical anecdotes; scrutinize historical case documentation for reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neuroscientific and experimental evidence for unconscious processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept of the 'unconscious' is contested but has been studied via implicit attitude measures, fMRI, PET, and other indirect tests; proponents of neuropsychoanalysis argue neuroscience provides a biological basis for unconscious emotional processing, while opponents say such findings render psychoanalytic theory obsolete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider converging evidence from cognitive and neuroscience methods on unconscious processing and transference; determine whether neuroscientific findings substantively support psychoanalytic constructs or merely map correlates without validating theoretical mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive/hermeneutic framing versus empirical science
rubrics_metrics.description: Paul Ricoeur and others characterize psychoanalysis as a form of textual interpretation or 'hermeneutics of suspicion', focusing on interpretive work rather than positivist experimental science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging psychoanalysis, be explicit whether the criterion is interpretive insight (hermeneutic value) or empirical efficacy; these are different standards and may both be relevant depending on the evaluative goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical significance and conventional evaluation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators argue that LTPP's observed effect sizes imply it is 'not worthwhile, at least in terms of the conventional ways of evaluating therapies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conventional thresholds for clinical significance, cost-effectiveness, and standardized outcome metrics when deciding whether a therapy is 'worthwhile'; examine whether statistical effects translate into meaningful patient-level benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socio-cultural and institutional critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques from Foucault, Deleuze, Guattari, Irigaray and others argue psychoanalysis as an institution embodies power relations, confessional techniques, and exclusions (e.g., gendered critiques such as phallogocentrism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include socio-cultural, feminist, and institutional analyses as part of comprehensive evaluation—assess ethical, power-related, and cultural consequences of psychoanalytic practice and institutional structures in addition to clinical and scientific metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and evidentiary scrutiny of foundational cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Some historical accusations (e.g., alleged fabrication in the Anna O. case) and reinterpretations (possible misdiagnosis such as tuberculous meningitis) challenge the evidentiary basis of early psychoanalytic claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject foundational case reports to historical-critical review and cross-checks with contemporary medical knowledge; consider how reinterpretation of key cases affects the plausibility of initial theoretical inferences.
